summary: יָם is the sea: the gathered waters God named on the third day, made, bounded and ruled by him (Gen 1:10; Exo 20:11; Job 38:8–11), and with a name a particular sea or lake, the Sea of Reeds, the Great Sea, the Salt Sea, Kinnereth. Since the Great Sea lies west of the land, יָם and יָמָּה are also “west, westward” (Num 34:6; Gen 13:14), and Solomon’s great cast basin was “the sea” (1Ki 7:23). In figure the sand of the sea is a countless multitude, and the roaring, restless sea is the peoples in tumult (Isa 17:12; 57:20), the sea out of which Daniel’s beasts rise (Dan 7:2–3; Rev 13:1; 17:15). Ugaritic ym, Phoenician ym and Aramaic יַמָּא share the word; Biblical Aramaic יַם and the Peshitta’s יַמָא belong to the entry.

words.gloss: (meaning uncertain) water found in the wilderness, perhaps hot springs
words.summary: Found once, of what Anah found in the wilderness while pasturing his father’s donkeys (Gen 36:24). The verse does not define it; something found in the wilderness by a herdsman suits a water source, but neither its meaning nor its tie to יָם “sea” is established, and no cognate has been found for it, so the root’s cognates count against it.

cognates.gloss: sea; Yamm, the sea as a god

evidence.note: “ym /yamm-/ ‘sea’, 1.2:IV:7 = 88.51 DN (perhaps also 1.4:IV:31 = 85.2) (H. yam, yamm-, Aram. yamma, Arab. yamm)”; set apart from ym /yôm-/ “day” in the entry before it.
“Lady Athirat of the Sea”.
“sea; Yam (god of the sea)”.

cognates.note: The doubled m (yamm-) agrees with the Hebrew plural יַמִּים and Aramaic יַמָּא. In the Baal cycle the sea is a god, Prince Yamm, whom Baal fights (KTU 1.2:IV); in scripture the sea is a thing God made and commands (Psa 95:5; Job 38:8–11).

evidence.note: “[Heb. yam] n.m. SEA”: KAI 14.16, 18 (Ph) ṣdn ʾrṣ ym, “Sidon, land of the sea”; KAI 51 Reverse 2, “governor of ḤRMN-on-sea”; KAI 145 I 4–6 (NPu), “I, Mescar, rule the seas (ymm)”. Entered apart from YM II “day”.
“open sea”.

cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic, the speech of the sea-going coast north of Israel: a coastal city is “land of the sea” and a ruler claims the seas.

evidence.note: ch. “same” (as Hebrew יָם “sea, lake, reservoir”): Targ. Gen. IX, 2; Targ. I Kings VII, 23; pl. יַמְמַיָּא, יַמַּיָּא, Targ. Gen. I, 10.
“sea”.

evidence.note: حَجَرًا مُلْقًى فِى اليَمِّ, “a stone thrown into the sea”, whence the case was also called يَمِّيَّة.
Refers to المُشَرَّكَةُ; Lane’s article يم has no separate entry for the noun.
“open sea”; “Borrowed from a Northwest Semitic language, most probably Aramaic ימא (yammā) or Hebrew יָם (yām).”

cognates.note: Arabic’s own word for the sea is baḥr; yamm is taken to be borrowed from Aramaic or Hebrew, so it is a witness to the word’s meaning, not an independent cognate.

evidence.locator: tla24730, ym “sea (Sem. loan word)” (Wb 1, 78.11; Hoch, Sem. Words, no. 52)

cognates.note: An Egyptian word borrowed from a Semitic language (the dictionary marks it “Sem. loan word”), the reverse of the usual direction: the Canaanite word for the sea in New Kingdom Egyptian.

doctrine.statement: On the third day God gathered the waters under the heavens into one place, let the dry land appear, and called the gathered waters יַמִּים, “seas” (Gen 1:9–10, 13). The fourth commandment names the sea among the works of the six days: “in six days Yahweh made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day” (Exo 20:11). The sea is his because he made it (Psa 95:5; Jon 1:9; Neh 9:6), and he set it a bound it cannot pass (Job 38:8–11; Pro 8:29; Jer 5:22). The apostles pray and preach in the same words, to God “who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them” (Act 4:24; 14:15; Rev 14:7). From the verses: the sea is no god and no primeval chaos but a thing made, on a named day of the creation week, and held in place by God’s decree ever since.

The Psalms give the stilling of the sea to God: he stills the roar of the seas (Psa 65:8), rules the surging of the sea and calms its waves (Psa 89:10), and makes the storm a calm (Psa 107:29). Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea and there was a great calm, and the men asked what man this was, that even the winds and the sea obey him (Mat 8:26–27). The crowds who saw his works glorified God, “who had given such authority to men” (Mat 9:8), and Jesus himself says, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Mat 28:18). From the verses: the power over the sea is God’s, and the son exercised it as one to whom his Father gave it.

Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground with the waters a wall on either side, and that day Yahweh saved Israel from the hand of Egypt (Exo 14:22, 29–30). Paul says that the fathers “all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea”, and adds that with most of them God was not pleased, for they fell in the wilderness (1Co 10:1–2, 5). From the verses: the passage through the sea is scripture’s own figure of baptism, a going through the water out of bondage into a new allegiance; and, as with the fathers, it begins the journey but does not finish it.

Isaiah sets the roar of many peoples beside the roaring of the seas (Isa 17:12), the psalmist God’s stilling of the seas beside his stilling of the tumult of the peoples (Psa 65:8), and “the abundance of the sea” beside “the wealth of the nations” (Isa 60:5); Ezekiel’s nations come up against Tyre as the sea brings up its waves (Ezk 26:3). The wicked are “like the driven sea, for it cannot rest”, and have no peace (Isa 57:20–21). Daniel sees the four winds stir up the great sea and four beasts come up out of it, and is told the beasts are four kings (Dan 7:2–3, 17). John sees a beast rise out of the sea and receive authority over every tribe, people, tongue and nation (Rev 13:1, 7), and is told that the waters he saw are “peoples and multitudes and nations and languages” (Rev 17:15). Jesus foretells “distress of nations” with the roaring of the sea (Luk 21:25). In the new heavens and new earth “the sea is no more” (Rev 21:1). From the verses: in prophecy the sea is the nations in their unrest, out of which the kingdoms of men arise; that the sea is no more means that, when God’s kingdom is established, the restless nations opposed to him are no more.

The king of Psalm 72 is to rule “from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth” (Psa 72:8), and Zechariah says the same of the king who comes to Zion lowly on a donkey, who will speak peace to the nations (Zec 9:9–10). In that day living waters will go out from Jerusalem to the eastern sea and to the western sea, and Yahweh will be king over all the earth (Zec 14:8–9); the waters going out from the temple heal the Salt Sea, so that fishermen spread their nets there and its fish are like the fish of the Great Sea (Ezk 47:8–10). The earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh “as the waters cover the sea” (Isa 11:9; Hab 2:14). From the verses: the kingdom is a reign on this earth, centred on Jerusalem, reaching to the seas that bound the land and to the ends of the earth, which God’s knowledge will fill.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. ROOT: the database keys יָם (j.br.ab) and יֵמִם (j.br.ac) under יממ, BDB’s heading j.br.aa (an assumed verb ימם with no tokens), so the entry’s root is יממ; no entry has that root (yom.json is יומ, its Syriac אִימָמָא is איממ; yamin.json is ימנ). Biblical Aramaic יַם (xj.ag.ab, Dan 7:2–3) is keyed ימ, given as its word root. The Peshitta words carry SEDRA’s root ימא (root 824: lexemes 1385 ימא ×108, 1386 ימתא ×11, 1387 ימא-דסופ ×2, the last entered as a phrase); SEDRA root 823 is a different ימא, “swear” (ימא, מומתא), and is not part of this entry. Syriac lemmas are copied from the database’s vocalised forms. j.br.aa is the root heading only and has no tokens. VERSE NUMBERS are the Hebrew text’s: Isa 8:23 = Eng 9:1; Hos 2:1 = 1:10; 1Ki 5:9 = 4:29; Gen 32:13 = 32:12; Psa 8:9 = 8:8; Psa 46:3 = 46:2; Psa 65:8 = 65:7; Psa 89:10 = 89:9; Psa 68:23 = 68:22. SENSES: Psa 107:3 and Isa 49:12 (“from the north and from the sea”) are not cited for “west”, since the sea there may be the south. Isa 21:1 “wilderness of the sea” is left unassigned. COGNATES: Segert’s page 188 is read from the OCR between the running heads 187 and 189 (the 188 head is missing); check the scan. Krahmalkov p. 208 is from the text layer. Akkadian: the sea-word is tiāmtu, which answers to תְּהוֹם, not to יָם, and no Akkadian yāmu was found in Oracc; Wiktionary’s Eblaite wamû “sea” and Proto-Semitic *wamm- are leads not followed to a dictionary. Ge'ez not consulted. Syriac dictionaries (Payne Smith) not consulted for ܝܡܐ beyond SEDRA. Arabic yamm is entered as a loan, following Wiktionary’s etymology. LEADS: Rev 4:6 and 15:2, the “sea of glass” before the throne, may answer to the temple’s cast sea; not asserted. The Peshitta renders Rev 19:20–21:8 “lake of fire” with יַמתָֿא. Open: the gloss and meaning of יֵמִם (Gen 36:24) remain uncertain; its negative balance reflects that. The doctrine ‘nations-as-the-sea’ states the Christadelphian reading of Rev 21:1 plainly; check its wording.
